senses.definition: (transitive) To tease someone in a kindly or friendly fashion.

quotes.text:
"My dear Polly. I welcome criticism, but this is mere——"
Lady Wetherby stroked his coat sleeve fondly.
"Never mind, Algie, I was only joshing you, precious.[…]"
quotes.reference: 1915, Pelham Grenville Wodehouse, Uneasy Money, New York, N.Y.: D. Appleton and Company, published 17 March 1916, →OCLC, page 171:

senses.definition: (intransitive) To make or exchange good-natured jokes.

quotes.text: We are old friends, did I not tell you? So I may, what you Americans call, josh with him.
quotes.reference: 1902, Jack London, chapter XIV, in A Daughter of the Snows:

quotes.text: “Cut that joshing out,” she said, coolly and briskly. “Who do you think you are talking to? Your check, please. Oh, Lordy!—”
quotes.reference: 1910, O. Henry [pseudonym; William Sydney Porter], “The Girl and the Habit”, in Strictly Business:

quotes.text: Boris, it seems, is taking it in this spirit, joshing beneath his ever-redeeming barnet that Labour's opposition to military action in Syria is a fey stance that he, as GQ politician of the year, would never be guilty of.
